Mr. Speaker, I should like to say only a few words on the motion for second reading of this very important bill now before us. All those who spoke before me emphasized the seriousness, the importance and the need of this bill. They also suggested that all members would unanimously agree at least on the principle of the bill under discussion.
Mr. Speaker, 1 understand that by passing this legislation, we shall repeal the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. This means that Bill C-100 includes certain provisions of the former act, as well as new ones. In this regard, I should like to point out to the house that this is the first time, to my knowledge, that a bill is submitted without any explanatory notes. I hope that the minister will give us some reason when he replies to our various remarks.
In fact, I noticed that when a new bill is introduced to amend an existing statute, we are always given explanatory notes, which greatly help us appreciate the extent of the proposed changes and the legislator's intentions. In my opinion, it is most unfortunate that this long bill, which has a great number of sections, should not also contain such notes. I would have appreciated it very much if it had been provided with explanatory notes; that would have been most helpful to us in understanding the importance of the changes which are proposed through these new provisions.
The second part of the bill introduces a new concept: preventive detention and custody for treatment. It is to be expected that such an innovation will call for an expansion program with respect to the construction of institutions and will entail, I think, federal-provincial agreements on the question. It was quite urgent that inmates who are drug addicts be separated from other criminals. So, the sooner we build those institutions for the custody and treatment of addicts, the better it will be for all concerned.
Narcotic Drugs Control
Mr. Speaker, without entering into all the details of this bill, since we will have an opportunity to deal with them in the committee of the whole, I glanced briefly at clause 8. Here, the minister recognizes the fact of possession as an offence under the law, so that if a person charged with drug traffic is brought before the court and the crown establishes the fact of possession, it will have established an offence on the part of the accused. Everyone knows that by making possession an offence the enforcement of an act such as this is made much easier.
I think the minister will appreciate the basic distinction between section 8 of Bill C-100 and a certain section of a bill which we discussed last night. But I do not wish to labour the point because I would be out of order and because the minister, having heard about it during hours last night, would not like to see me take that course again.
Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) was telling us, in his statement, that this new act, including these new provisions, was being substituted for an act which had not proved as effective as expected. I do not think such an assertion is justified on the part of the minister.
Crime as much as society changes with the years and laws that have been of great value for us in the past have to be amended in the light of changing conditions. I feel that we have here an instance of that. This new act, embodying new concepts, is being introduced to meet new requirements. I readily agree with the principle of the bill; I am glad this legislation has been introduced and I am sure it will be very effective.
I understand that severe penalties are provided for the supplying of imported narcotic drugs. Provision is made for the treatment of addicts. On this matter of drug addict treatment, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) asked the minister earlier to consider the possibility for those whose addiction reduces them to slavery to be treated without being taken before the courts. On that point, I should like to quote a few lines from an editorial which appeared in La Presse for Wednesday, May 31:
-at the same time, the victims of that traffic who become addicted to drugs should properly be considered as ill. They are less guilty than the traffickers and are more in need of treatment than of punishment. However, it is not enough to pass good legislation. The laws must be enforced with severity in the case of criminals and with humanity in the case of sick people.
5998	HOUSE OF
Narcotic Drugs Control
Mr. Speaker, this problem created by the use of drugs is obviously very serious. It is said to be more serious in the Vancouver area, but I am not too sure of that, nor am I sure of the accuracy of the statistics quoted by the minister a moment ago. When it comes to narcotics, there are no statistics that can give a complete idea of the extent of the damage caused in this country. I am quite sure that every large city, Toronto just as much as Montreal-which is a seaport-are exposed to the evils of this scourge.
This bill also provides for the rehabilitation and re-education of those afflicted with what I would call this disease.
Even if we pass this bill, which we will try to improve when the details are considered in committee, it will not be enough. An educational campaign will have to be launched to warn the public, and particularly the young people, against the danger of this social evil of drug addiction.
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed cases where responsibility varies as between importers, traffickers or users of narcotics.
As far as I am concerned, we can never deal too harshly with those who knowingly and deliberately engage in the importation of such drugs, which are a plague to society and to many of our homes. Nor can we ever be too hard on traffickers, people who, while trafficking in narcotics, are usually smart enough not to use them themselves, but prey on the misery and enslavement of others.
Personally, I think we should provide the severest punishment for those two classes of criminals.
Our primary responsibility here is to pass legislation to protect society, decent people and particularly our young people.
I feel sure every hon. member will want to take this opportunity to make the law as strict as possible, so that those responsible for this scourge that victimizes so many Canadians will be subject to the most severe punishment.

speechtext:
I wish to take the opportunity at this time to deal with this very important bill, a measure which is of particular significance to those hon. members who come from the lower mainland of British Columbia.


It has been indicated that there are between 3,000 and 5,000 drug addicts in Canada at the present time and that some 1,500 or 2,000 of them are in the greater Vancouver area. These addicts require some $30 a day to spend on their drug habit which is the equivalent of $10,000 a year, or the entire salary of a member of parliament devoted entirely to the purchase of drugs. If a further calculation is made on the basis of 2,000 drug addicts we arrive at a figure of approximately $20 million a year being spent on drugs, and if we further consider that the majority of these people have to steal in order to provide for their habit and that stolen goods only realize one third of their true value, we reach a figure of some $60 million a year. Perhaps this figure is high, because of the fact that many of the addicts are in prison or capable of "tapering off" at intervals, but the calculation is enough to show that the problem is an extremely serious one viewed from the financial aspect alone.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) and myself took the opportunity during the last recess to visit the New Westminster penitentiary and I was impressed by the work that warden Hall was doing despite the handicap imposed by the intermixing with the rest of the prison population of the 25 per cent who are drug addicts. I think one positive step which the present bill takes is the provision made for the segregation of drug addicts. We also took the opportunity to visit the Oakalla prison farm and again we saw an excellent job being done by warden Hugh Christie in the face of tremendous handicaps. A separate establishment is provided there for women drug addicts and the officials are engaged in an excellent rehabilitation campaign. I emphasize these positive aspects of the work which is presently being done despite the handicaps imposed by shortage of accommodation and so on. One point which has not been emphasized is the higher than average level of intelligence possessed by most drug addicts. In order to provide for the satisfaction of their habit they are obliged to be "on the go" literally night and day. Even when an addict is put into a penitentiary or a prison farm this activity continues, and despite all the precautions taken large quantities of drugs are smuggled in. There have been instances where drugs have been concealed in the shoes of children visiting their parents. In other cases, books have been brought in, certain pages of which had been soaked with a particular drug. The prisoner would secure the book and retire to his cell, extract the drug and usually manage to get the necessary material for a fix. I mention this to show that the

addict presents a most difficult problem; the fact that the present bill provides for his segregation goes a long way.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has deplored the fact that no voluntary treatment centres for drug addicts are to be provided, yet he did mention the narcotic addict foundation of British Columbia which was started in 1955. At the present time it is under the direction of Dr. Robert Halliday who is doing outstanding work in the treatment of addicts who attend voluntarily. He is assisted by a capable board of directors, the chairman being Mr. John Carson. This foundation treats both in patients and out patients, besides providing for rehabilitation, education and research. I do not think we can consider the provisions of this particular bill in isolation. It provides for the penal aspects of this problem and for the treatment of addicts caught in the crime net; I think it should go forward side by side with the development of an organization such as the narcotic addict foundation of British Columbia which has done the pioneer work and now needs substantial funds in order to expand its operations.
I think that one important aspect of this work which has been neglected is the tremendous amount of research work which is needed. I was concerned when the minister told us that this new institution contemplated would be placed somewhere on the lower mainland. This provides a considerable amount of latitude. I think it is important that this treatment centre should be located right in the community where most drug addicts are to be found and that it should also be located close to the universities where skilled and qualified people are available to undertake the necessary research tasks. If the buildings are put up in some outlying region I suggest that qualified personnel will not be available to deal with this problem.
Here is an interesting thing about the Vancouver area. It is true we have the highest rate of addiction in Canada. We also have the highest rates of suicide, divorce, illegitimacy, delinquency, alcoholism and admission to mental hospitals. I doubt if the tourist association will be too happy about this recommendation, but I think it indicates there is a high degree of correlation between drug addiction and other social diseases. The only social studies we have had so far in Canada have been one made in 1955 by the special Senate committee dealing with drug addiction and a report by Mr. Stevenson, I believe, in 1956. I suggest that the sociological aspect of research in regard to literature available has been negligible.
I should also like to suggest that the location of the centres should be at those points
Narcotic Drugs Control where the drug addiction problem is greatest. The primary one would of course be located in the city of Vancouver with a second and third located at Toronto and Montreal. I suggest they be established close to universities and regular community facilities. That particular plan has been followed by the narcotic foundation which has found it to be successful in respect to both in and out patients.
There is one other aspect of the present legislation with which I am particularly concerned dealing with the matter of trafficking.
I do not feel that the provision for life imprisonment is sufficient and that there should be included in the provisions of this act the death sentence as an alternative. I make that suggestion because I feel that those individuals dealing in narcotic trafficking are perhaps committing a worse type of murder-destruction of the social entity of victims they introduce to use of narcotics-than the types of murder for which we have provided sentences by recent amendments to the Criminal Code.
I think this type of crime is described quite accurately in an article which appeared in Life magazine for February 1, 1960. The article relates to world crime syndicates and reads as follows:
But whatever their corporate structure and whatever their number of employees, international criminals in all fields share certain common attitudes. They are interested in big, quick profits. They are contemptuous of the laws they so adroitly evade. They are indifferent to the suffering and hardship that they spread throughout the world.
At the top of the roster stands the most extensive, most effective criminal agency in the western world, the widely known and widely misunderstood Mafia. Many people are convinced that the Mafia is a colossus of crime with branch offices in every major city and an I.B.M.-like efficiency. Some people are convinced that the Mafia, if it ever existed at all, does not exist now. Both groups are mistaken.
The Mafia does exist. But instead of being a world-wide syndicate, it operates almost entirely in its birthplace, Sicily, and in its adopted home, the United States. It does have a few branch offices on the Italian mainland and in certain centres of the narcotics trade but scarcely a single representative anywhere else. It does have a kind of organization but not a very tightknit one. The Mafia is principally a way of life shared by groups of lawbreakers who understand and trust one another and who work together for mutual safety.
This work is crime-usually dirty crime. As reported in last week's article, the Mafia is the principal conductor of the world's cruelest business, the narcotics traffic.
I feel it is also of interest to note that in January of last year, or some time prior to that, many of the type of people that belong to the Mafia held what has been called the Appalachian conference. The major topic for discussion at that particular conference had to do with that crime syndicate getting out of the narcotic traffic business. I suggest the reason that syndicate decided to cease its
6000	HOUSE OF
Narcotic Drugs Control narcotic operation is because enforcement is becoming effective and the imposition of sentence is being extended.
I suggest that by this legislation we are aiming at the type of individual who is a kingpin in the drug traffic business, and the trafficker who is not a user of drugs himself, and I feel that the death sentence should be provided as an alternative to life imprisonment. I suggest that, because I am unable to see the necessity or justification for the state maintaining that type of individual at a cost of $2,000 per year which, applied to a life sentence of 10 or 20 years, would amount to $20,000 or $40,000 respectively.
In the field of medicine today cancerous areas of the body are removed for the protection of the remaining living tissue. I suggest in respect of the narcotics trafficking field, that traffickers who do not use narcotics can be likened to cancerous tissue and should be permanently removed.
Mr. Speaker, in the Globe and Mail of November 19, I960 there appeared an article under the heading "Dope Pushers Face Death". The following statement appears under the dateline Bangkok, November 16: Heroin and morphine manufacturers and peddlers face the death sentence or life imprisonment under a bill approved by the Thai cabinet today.
I suggest that indicates that other countries are dealing with this particular problem in an effective way.
During the introduction of this bill the minister indicated concern not only in its narrow aspect in Canada but also in the need for strengthening international enforcement.
I was interested to hear the hon. member for Vancouver East refer to the rather low per capita addiction in the United Kingdom. It has been suggested by some sources that those figures which he quoted are not too accurate because of the lack of supervision and availability of narcotics, and that the actual per capita number of addicts to opium in the United Kingdom is much higher than in Canada.
I should also like to draw to the attention of the hon. members of this house the fact that one of the largest processing countries of narcotic drugs is France, in the areas of Paris and Marseilles. Morphine is processed by laboratories there into refined heroin, yet there is practically no addiction problem in France. I suggest that the wholesale centre of the world for narcotics is located in Milan, Italy. It is estimated there are some 2,000 individuals employed in the wholesale narcotic business in that locality yet Italy does not have a drug addiction problem.
The point I have tried to make is that since we have concluded that life imprisonment is a deterrent, the penalty should be 

increased further because, as the hon. member for Vancouver East pointed out, the worst type of murder should carry the death penalty, to be meted out at the discretion of the court or the judge.
In respect of the locations of the treatment centres I suggest steps should be taken to ensure that they are located in the centre of communities rather than in the outlying areas. I suggest also that provision should be made for more extensive research on the part of voluntary organizations through which voluntary treatment can be obtained. An example of the type of organization to which I refer can be found in the narcotic addict foundation. That type of organization should be encouraged to develop, and I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will devote a portion of his budget to providing greater subsidies to those organizations which are now doing such excellent work on budgets of some $200,000 to $300,000.
I should also like to see consideration given to Canada's active participation in Interpol in an attempt to prevent narcotics coming into this country. I suggest we are concerned with the world-wide aspect of this problem and should, therefore, provide every co-operation, both financial and moral, in order to curtail this very vicious racket.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much time now, in view of the fact that we will be discussing the bill in some detail when we reach consideration in committee. However, I should like to make a few remarks as a result of speeches made by various hon. members during second reading stage. I was pleased, of course, to hear the enthusiastic-I think I can call it that-response of all hon. members who have spoken despite the fact that there were some things in connection with the suggestions with which we may not agree. I know that some of the suggestions were made with the best of intentions and in order to strengthen the bill further as hon. members see it.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) spoke of the fact that the intent of the bill appeared to be to deal firmly but kindly with addicts and that this was inherent in the bill. We believe this to be so.

I should like to say I am well aware of the keen interest which the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has had in this subject for many years. I realize his strong feelings. I should like to say how much I appreciate his words with respect to Canada's part in the conference at New York recently and his gratifying words concerning Mr. Robert Curran of my department. He said that I indicated that the treaty would be presented to parliament for ratification. What I actually said was, "I am happy to be able to say that Canada not only played an active and important role in the conference but is now taking the necessary steps to be in a position subject to the approval of parliament, to ratify the convention." I am given to understand that external affairs is now actually processing the convention but I am also of the impression-I may not be correct in this-that, following the examination by external affairs, an order in council may be sufficient rather than an actual presentation of the convention to the House of Commons.
I may have given the wrong impression in my opening remarks Mr. Speaker, in that it is my understanding that the major suppliers of legal opium for medical use are India and Turkey. I can give more details on that matter when we get into committee.
I am pleased that the matter of doctors and the use of legal narcotics by the medical profession has arisen. I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that sections 6 and 16 of the present act set out the circumstances under which a physician may administer or prescribe drugs and the circumstances wherein it is improper for him to do so.
It has been the subject of some criticism that the legislation should attempt in any way to define what is or is not proper professional treatment and practice. It has, of course, been the view of the department that the legislation does not attempt this. Nevertheless there has been a strong feeling by many members of the profession that this is the interpretation to be given to those sections and that no professional man should be called upon to decide whether he is or is not breaking the law in a matter involving his professional conscience and the treatment of a patient under his care. The bill, therefore, makes no reference to what constitutes legal employment of drugs by a professional person. The regulations, however, will cover this by providing that a medical practitioner may prescribe, administer or furnish a narcotic to a person if such person is a patient under his professional treatment and the narcotic is required for the condition for which the patient is receiving treatment. We feel this represents an important change in language,
Narcotic Drugs Control if not in principle, to that contained in sections 6 and 16 of the present act. This is thought to be a desirable change in that it leaves to professional interpretation what is or is not a proper use of a narcotic. Actually, we hope to encourage doctors to take more responsibility for and interest in the health and well-being of the addict. We can, of course, go into that in more detail in committee, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for London (Mr. Hal-penny) gave a detailed description of the legal use of narcotics. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) mentioned the fact that there were no explanatory notes to this bill. It is my understanding that no explanatory notes are necessary when it is a new bill. For instance, Bill No. C-71 respecting the civil service of Canada deals with legislation that we have had for a great many years. But it is new legislation. There are no explanatory notes to Bill No. C-71. I am told this is the reason why explanatory notes have been omitted here in the case of the narcotic bill.
When we are examining the bill in committee I shall be very glad to give the origin of each clause in relation to the present act, if the clause is not new.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale) mentioned another matter which the hon. member for Vancouver East had brought into the discussion. I think I should like to make a short statement on what has been called the British narcotics system. There is a great deal of popular misconception regarding the so-called British narcotics system, and I am glad this question has been raised because it gives me an opportunity to place on record the actual situation.
Whenever proposals are advanced respecting the problem of narcotic addiction the question that is almost invariably asked is why do we not try the British system. In the first place, I should like to assure hon. members that there is no such thing as the British system. The legislation in the United Kingdom does not differ in purpose or subject matter from the legislation in Canada. If anything, our legislation permits of more effective control, and in so far as trafficking is concerned, of more severe penalties.
It is not correct to say that in the United Kingdom addicts can get all the narcotics that they require from their family doctor. Doctors, in accordance with their professional judgment, are permitted to furnish narcotics to persons requiring such medication. This does not differ from the situation covered by the legislation which is before the house. Doctors in the United Kingdom are not per-mited to furnish narcotics indiscriminately or indefinitely to addicts; neither would doctors
6002	HOUSE OF
Narcotic Drugs Control be permitted to do so under this legislation. There is, accordingly, no difference in so far as the legal use of narcotics is concerned under the United Kingdom legislation and this legislation.
We feel that our methods of reporting and recording narcotic transactions covering legal distribution, coupled with the knowledge and experience of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, give us a very accurate picture of the narcotic situation in Canada and particularly as it relates to what are called criminal addicts. I would not like to draw any comparison between our methods of recording and reporting and those in force in the United Kingdom, but I am satisfied that our methods will favourably stand up to any comparison that can be made.
This becomes of some importance in trying to explain why we have some 3,000 criminal addicts in Canada whereas the United Kingdom authorities report a number fewer than 200. Regardless of whether the United Kingdom methods if applied to Canada would reflect with the same accuracy our numbers of addicts, we are satisfied that because there does not exist a criminal underworld narcotic traffic in the United Kingdom, the number of addicts is very substantially less than ours on a per capita basis.
Through the R.C.M.P. we have made intensive inquiries in the United Kingdom and have also studied reports of other investigations into this very aspect of the problem. The general view that is expressed is that while there exists a criminal underworld element in the United Kingdom the narcotic addict is considered to be at the lowest level and it follows that the narcotic trafficker is regarded as beyond the pale of even criminal society. Why this is so may perhaps lie in the mores and culture of the United Kingdom which is a far more homogeneous society than that of North America. Apart from this, there is simply no explanation that wholly explains the difference in the two situations. I can assure hon. members that our inability to explain the difference in a more satisfactory manner is not for want of studying the situation in both countries, and even the United Kingdom authorities are not able to give any better explanation than the one I have given.
As a matter of interest, the explanation I have given, in addition to being based on our own knowledge, is also based upon the report of a special study that was made by senior health officers of the New York state department of health who went to the United Kingdom for the express purpose of finding out something about the so-called British system and as a result they have reported that there is no such thing.


In conclusion, I should like to set at rest once and for all the misconception that the success of the British system, if there was such a thing, lies in the furnishing of legal narcotics to narcotic addicts. This is no more tolerated as a general practice in the United Kingdom than would be the case in Canada.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond mentioned the narcotic addiction foundation of British Columbia. I have their most recent report here. I have been studying it and I should like to mention that it is a very comprehensive study. I do not think there is anything more that I can say at this time. As I mentioned earlier, my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), and I will do our best to give as complete explanations as possible when we get into committee on the bill, and I should again like to express my appreciation of the constructive approach which has been taken on both sides of the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
May I inquire from the ministers whether there is contemplated any possibility of treating people within penitentiaries as they are now constituted? The Minister of Justice said that an institution was to be established in southern British Columbia. He did not indicate whether it would be an institution of a type similar to a regular
Narcotic Drugs Control penitentiary or whether it would be more in the nature of a hospital to treat narcotic addiction.
The question just asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East points up the necessity of having something more than just a prison where these people can be treated. If there is any possibility at all now or in the future of addicts entering voluntarily for treatment,
I would assume it would be against the interests of society and against the interests of the addict to put the addict in a prison rather than a hospital if he has not been convicted of any offence. Therefore, until narcotic hospitals of some sort can be provided there would be no facilities for voluntary entrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
That is correct. What is contemplated here is the establishment of institutions to which people are committed for custody and for treatment. Under the new bill they will be committed as the result of a charge of possession or trafficking or importing. If they are then found to be addicts, they will be committed as a result of the criminal procedure.
The program envisaged in this bill contemplates also that the provinces may pass complementary legislation providing for committal to that institution of persons who need treatment. What my hon. friend from Vancouver East is referring to is something different, something which would go beyond that and would make provision for a person whose addiction is perhaps not so serious that he requires committal to custody for treatment. There would be, rather, an institution to which he may go voluntarily on terms arranged between himself and the institution. My colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and his department, do have in mind the possibility of assistance to the provinces in setting up such institutions, call them what you will, hospitals, drug hospitals or treatment centres, to which persons might go voluntarily. There would be absent from these institutions the element of custody, as it is envisaged in this bill, custody for treatment.
The reason why I think such institutions would have to be quite separate, and why I think the person desiring voluntary treatment should not go to the institution contemplated by this bill, is that the institution to which persons are committed to custody for treatment obviously has to be operated under a regimen. This bill and the new Penitentiary Act together make provision for such institutions to be operated, in fact, under the authority of the Penitentiary Act. Release will only be permitted when the parole board says it is in the interest of society to release the inmates. You will see that there is

Narcotic Drugs Control definitely an element of custody, although the purpose of the custody is treatment. It would not be, in our view, convenient nor would it be acceptable to persons wishing to go to an institution where they are voluntary patients, to have them in the same place where, in fact, you must have a regimen and where the period during which persons stay there is not subject to their own desires but is set by authority. I do not think you can have the two types of institution run together, nor do I think you can have the two types of inmates there, one group who are there voluntarily and can leave anytime they want and the other group who are there in custody and can only leave when the parole board certifies it is in the public interest for them to do so.
A different kind of institution would be necessary to meet the case put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Niagara Falls. As I have said, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his department have instituted some discussions with the provinces to explore the possibility of federal-provincial cooperation in the setting up of such institutions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I just cannot see that argument. If a person is an addict then, of necessity, that person has a quantity of narcotic in his or her possession almost daily; that is axiomatic. I do not know the exact figure now, but two or three years ago the majority of the women in the women's section of the Kingston penitentiary were from British Columbia. They were not there as a result of a charge of being in possession but because they were addicts. I imagine the same situation prevails now. They require treatment.
What is the difference in approach under this new plan? These women are there not because they participated in a bank robbery, or for breaking and entering or for prostitution, they are there because they are addicts. What is the difference, then, between the person who has been placed in custody under this new law and someone who voluntarily goes to an institution for treatment? They both require exactly the same thing. Is it not, in some sense, a duplication to have two such institutions? We are going to need very experienced personnel in connection with this particular program. I appreciate that there may be a different approach to the person who volunteers for treatment, but why have two such institutions when the purpose is the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Because of the essential difference to which my hon. friend has just

referred; that one group would be in the institution for treatment because they went there voluntarily, and the other group would be in the institution because they were committed either as a result of a criminal trial or under the appropriate provincial legislation. I am sure if my hon. friend stops to reflect, he will appreciate that it would be, first, unacceptable to persons who wanted to go to an institution voluntarily for treatment to go to one run by the penitentiaries branch and where necessarily, if unfortunately, the atmosphere is that of a place where persons are committed under the Criminal Code. People simply would not go to that institution voluntarily and, with respect, I do not think it is sensible to suggest they would. This type of institution we conclude, therefore, should be designed to house those persons who are committed under our federal law or under the appropriate provincial legislation when it is passed. Persons who, recognizing they are drug addicts and wanting to take treatment, but also to retain their freedom, we hope will before too long find other institutions to which they can go voluntarily.
The best distinction would be that a hospital is a place to which a person ordinarily goes voluntarily because he knows that he is sick or his doctor tells him he should go to hospital. He can leave, within certain unimportant limitations, whenever he desires. However, a mental hospital, for instance, in most cases is a place to which a person is committed under the appropriate provincial legislation because the legislators have said: in our view a person who is suffering from mental disease may be such that it is in society's interest that he be committed to a mental institution until such time as he may be cured. In the kind of mental institution of which I am thinking, the people are not there voluntarily and they are not free to leave whenever they wish. It seems to me that is about the best illustration I can find of the difference between the institution contemplated under this bill, where the inmate is not there voluntarily, he is not free to decide for himself whether he will leave, and the other type of institution about which my hon. friend is talking which would be necessary to serve a person who, recognizing his own illness and not having been convicted of any offence or not having been committed under provincial legislation, simply wants to go to an institution for treatment. I do not think you can mix the two kinds of institution, physically or even under one administration.

speechtext:
I just want to support the remarks of my colleague the hon. member for 90205-6-379
Narcotic Drugs Control Burnaby-Richmond and also those of the hon. member for Vancouver East. After all, this is very much a Vancouver problem. Hon. members on all sides of the house agree that this bill is a major step forward and that the ministers are to be commended. However, there seems to be a gap in one spot namely, in the line of voluntary commitment and also along the lines of drugs being supplied through an out-patient clinic or through a federally administered operation at cost where these drugs are required by the addict and where medical opinion says that the man cannot be reduced below this minimum level as far as drugs are concerned.
The question of the profit factor or of taking the profit factor out is extremely important and this in effect would tend to do that. What we want to do is to get at the people who are traffickers and who are creating new addicts daily. These are the people who have expanded this pool of drug addicts to its present size. The bill takes care of those people we are going to put in the penitentiary. But what about the people who should be treated as sick persons, as is the intent of this legislation, in an out-patient type of clinic where they go voluntarily and where there is no control? Where this post sentence rehabilitation takes place we are going to have social workers or case workers looking after these penitentiary inmates when they get out in order to try to rehabilitate them. Here you have a person who has not gone to penitentiary, a person who has an even better chance of rehabilitation than has the person who has had to be sent to a penitentiary. It seems to me that this is within the area of concern of the department of national welfare. The minister more or less points this out in his remarks. He says this will be in agreement, in consultation and in co-operation with the provinces. But at the same time the federal government is taking the lead in this matter and I should like to see the federal government perhaps carrying it a little bit further. It may work a little bit faster and better than it would with the particular government we have today in British Columbia. I do not want to make this a political matter. This bill has been non-political all the way through. We all agree that it is good. We all agree that it is a marvellous step forward. However, there seems to be a bit of a gap in that field of taking care of what you might call the person who is just starting to become a drug addict, the person who comes along and voluntarily says, "I am going to reform" but who needs help, if you like-
